subject: Science
title: Animal babies
objectives: Children will match animal babies to their mothers.
Children will say that mothers care for their babies.
content: Matching animal babies to their mothers, eggs and chicks, and how mothers care for babies.
teachingActivities: Use the baby names chick, kid, calf, puppy and kitten with real or picture examples; link to human babies and mothers; use gentle language and soft toys.
learnerActivities: Match animal babies to their mothers and say that mothers care for babies.
resources: Picture pairs: hen and chick, goat and kid, cow and calf, dog and puppy, cat and kitten
assessment: Observe whether each child matches at least three animal babies to their mothers.
expectedOutcomes: Matches at least three animal babies to their mothers.

lessons.title: Mothers and babies
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Children will match animal babies to their mothers.
successCriteria: Matches a baby to its mother
Says the baby name with support
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can match animals to their homes and name many animals.
resources: Picture pairs: hen and chick, goat and kid, cow and calf
lessons.starter: Show a hen and say "This is a mother hen. Where is her baby?" Show the chick.
teacherActivities: Show each mother and baby pair and say both names.
Mix up the cards and show a mother. Ask "Where is the baby?"
Say the baby names together: chick, kid, calf.
Let each child take a card and find its pair.
learnerActivities: Children look and say the names.
Child points to the baby.
Children say the names.
Child finds the pair.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show each mother and baby pair and say both names. Children: Children look and say the names.
Step 2. Teacher: Mix up the cards and show a mother. Ask "Where is the baby?" Children: Child points to the baby.
Step 3. Teacher: Say the baby names together: chick, kid, calf. Children: Children say the names.
Step 4. Teacher: Let each child take a card and find its pair. Children: Child finds the pair.

practical.title: Mother and baby
steps: Each child picks a mother and finds its baby.
practical.safety: Use large soft cards. Supervise sharing and keep the floor clear.

differentiation.support: Offer two cards and say the mother and baby names.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to name another baby animal.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

questions.question: What is the baby of a hen?
What is the baby of a cow?

lessons.conclusion: Put the babies with their mothers and say goodnight.
lessons.homeConnection: Talk about baby animals when you see them or in pictures.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "match animal babies to their mothers" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

learnerFacing.songOrRhyme: Mother hen, baby chick. Mother goat, baby kid.

lessons.title: Eggs and chicks
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Children will learn that chicks hatch from eggs.
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can match animals to their homes and name many animals.
resources: Pictures of an egg, a cracking egg and a chick
lessons.starter: Show the toy egg and say "There is a baby inside. Crack, crack. Out comes a chick."
teacherActivities: Show the three pictures in order and tell the story of a chick hatching.
Open the toy egg to show the chick inside.
Act out hatching by curling up and then stretching out.
Let each child put the three pictures in order.
learnerActivities: Children watch and say egg, crack, chick.
Children look and say chick.
Children curl up and stretch out.
Child places the pictures in order with support.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show the three pictures in order and tell the story of a chick hatching. Children: Children watch and say egg, crack, chick.
Step 2. Teacher: Open the toy egg to show the chick inside. Children: Children look and say chick.
Step 3. Teacher: Act out hatching by curling up and then stretching out. Children: Children curl up and stretch out.
Step 4. Teacher: Let each child put the three pictures in order. Children: Child places the pictures in order with support.

practical.title: Hatching chick
steps: Curl up like an egg on the floor.
practical.safety: Clear the floor and keep children apart so they do not bump. Do not use real eggs.

differentiation.support: Curl up together and stretch out slowly.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to tell what comes first and last.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

questions.question: What comes out of an egg?

expectedOutcomes: Says that chicks come from eggs
lessons.conclusion: Put the chick back in the nest and whisper goodnight.
lessons.homeConnection: Look at a picture of a hen and chicks with your child.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "learn that chicks hatch from eggs" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: How mothers care
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Children will say how animal and human mothers care for their babies.
successCriteria: Says one way a mother cares for a baby
Acts out caring for a baby
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can match animals to their homes and name many animals.
lessons.starter: Hold a mother toy and baby toy and say "Mother cares for the baby. She gives food and keeps it warm."
teacherActivities: Show each picture and say what the mother does: feeds, keeps warm, protects.
Act out feeding and keeping the baby warm with the toys.
Ask "How does a mother care for her baby?"
Talk about how we care for a baby at home.
learnerActivities: Children look and say the words.
Children copy with their own toys.
Child says or shows one way.
Child shares an idea.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show each picture and say what the mother does: feeds, keeps warm, protects. Children: Children look and say the words.
Step 2. Teacher: Act out feeding and keeping the baby warm with the toys. Children: Children copy with their own toys.
Step 3. Teacher: Ask "How does a mother care for her baby?" Children: Child says or shows one way.
Step 4. Teacher: Talk about how we care for a baby at home. Children: Child shares an idea.

practical.title: Caring play
steps: Give each child a toy baby and a blanket.
Pretend to feed and keep it warm.
practical.safety: Use soft toys and be gentle. Remind children that real baby animals are touched only with an adult.

differentiation.support: Act out caring together and say the words.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to say how mothers keep babies safe.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

questions.question: What does a mother give her baby?
How do we keep a baby warm?

expectedOutcomes: Says how mothers care for babies
lessons.conclusion: Put the babies to bed and say "Sleep well."
lessons.homeConnection: Talk about how your family cares for a baby.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "say how animal and human mothers care for their babies" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Baby animal game
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Children will play a matching and naming game with baby animals.
successCriteria: Matches five baby animals to mothers
Names at least three baby animals
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can match animals to their homes and name many animals.
resources: Five mother and five baby cards
lessons.starter: Say "Mothers and babies are mixed up. Can you help them find each other?"
teacherActivities: Spread the mother cards out and give each child a baby card.
Say "Find your mother" and let children match.
Check each pair and say the names together.
learnerActivities: Children hold a baby card.
Child puts the baby on the right mother.
Children say the pair names.
Child matches a new pair.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Spread the mother cards out and give each child a baby card. Children: Children hold a baby card.
Step 2. Teacher: Say "Find your mother" and let children match. Children: Child puts the baby on the right mother.
Step 3. Teacher: Check each pair and say the names together. Children: Children say the pair names.
Step 4. Teacher: Swap cards and play again. Children: Child matches a new pair.

practical.title: Find your mother
steps: Put mother cards on the floor.
Give each child a baby card.
Find the mother and place the card.
practical.safety: Use large soft cards and keep the floor clear. Supervise turns.

differentiation.support: Use three pairs and name the baby first.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to match all five pairs alone.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

questions.question: Who is the mother of the kid?
Who is the baby of the dog?

expectedOutcomes: Matches five baby animals to mothers
lessons.conclusion: Put the cards away and say "Mothers and babies together."
lessons.homeConnection: Look at animal families in pictures or videos at home.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "play a matching and naming game with baby animals" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Week 3 babies check
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Teachers will observe how each child matches baby animals to mothers.
successCriteria: Matches at least three baby animals to mothers
Says that mothers care for babies
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can match animals to their homes and name many animals.
lessons.starter: Sing the mother and baby song and show three stations.
teacherActivities: Set up three stations: pairs, eggs and chicks, and caring.
At each station ask "Who is the baby?" and "How does the mother care?"
Record each child’s level and take photographs.
learnerActivities: Children rotate every four minutes.
Child answers with a word or gesture.
Children tidy at the signal.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Set up three stations: pairs, eggs and chicks, and caring. Children: Children rotate every four minutes.
Step 2. Teacher: At each station ask "Who is the baby?" and "How does the mother care?" Children: Child answers with a word or gesture.
Step 3. Teacher: Record each child’s level and take photographs. Children: Children tidy at the signal.

practical.title: Baby stations
practical.safety: Supervise each station and keep floors clear. Use soft toys and large cards.

differentiation.support: Provide an adult partner and use two pairs.
differentiation.extension: Ask a confident child to tell a friend about animal babies.

assessment.method: Observe and record Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding for: matches babies to mothers; names a baby animal; says how a mother cares.

questions.question: What is the baby of a hen?
What does a mother do?
questions.expected: Feeds and cares for the baby.

expectedOutcomes: Has an observation record for Week 3
lessons.conclusion: Wave goodbye to the mothers and babies.
lessons.homeConnection: Talk about mothers and babies at home.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "Teachers will observe how each child matches baby animals to mothers" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?
